data.long_meaning: From the Greek word xenos, meaning stranger or foreigner, and philia, meaning love. Xenophila represents a deep appreciation and kindness towards those who are different from us. The name Xenophila carries the meaning “Love of strangers” and is chosen by families in Christian traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Biblical tradition and is also used in English, Hebrew, Greek. Parents who choose Xenophila usually hope their child will grow to embody love of strangers and live with faith, good character and purpose.

in_hebrew.name: זנופילה
in_hebrew.long_meaning: השם זנופילה מורכב משתי מילים ביוונית: 'זנוס' (זרים) ו'פילה' (אהבה). הוא מתאר אדם שאוהב ומקבל זרים, תכונה חשובה במיוחד בקרב המאמינים הנוצרים שמדגישים את האהבה והקבלה של כולם.

in_greek.name: Ξενοφíλα
in_greek.long_meaning: Το όνομα Ξενοφíλα προέρχεται από τις ελληνικές λέξεις 'ξένος' (stranger) και 'φίλος' (αγάπη). Στην Καινή Διαθήκη, η έννοια της φιλοξενίας και της αγάπης προς τους ξένους είναι κεντρική, αντανακλώντας την πνευματική σημασία του ονόματος στη χριστιανική παράδοση.

in_latin.name: Xenophila
in_latin.long_meaning: Nomen Xenophila derivatur ex vocibus Graecis 'xenos' (alienus) et 'phila' (amor). In ecclesia primitiva Christiana, virtus hospitalitatis et caritatis erga peregrinos magnopere emphasizabatur, quae est spiritus proprietas nominis Xenophilae.

in_english.name: Xenophila
in_english.long_meaning: The name Xenophila originates from Greek roots 'xenos' (stranger) and 'phila' (love). It signifies a person who loves and welcomes strangers, reflecting a core Christian value of hospitality and love towards all, especially those who are different or from elsewhere. Historically, this trait was highly valued in early Christian communities.

historical_references.reference: Xenophila was a Christian martyr who suffered persecution during the reign of the Roman Emperor Diocletian (284-305 AD). She was a Roman noblewoman who converted to Christianity and was tortured for her faith, ultimately being beheaded.

Xenophila is also known as Xenophia of Thessalonica, and her life is recorded in the Acts of the Martyrs. She is believed to have lived during the early Christian period, and was a wealthy woman who used her wealth to support the Christian community in Thessalonica, Greece. When the city was sacked by the Heruli in 267 AD, Xenophila was taken captive and offered to be released if she would renounce her faith. She refused and was tortured and ultimately beheaded.
